title: The economy: power behind everyday life
title_zh: 经济：日常生活背后的力量
theme: economy, unemployment, economic bubbles, the sharing economy

section_a.question: What was the consequence when large numbers of homeowners failed to repay their loans?
options: The companies that owned the loans and their shareholders lost sizable amounts of money.
The price of houses rose sharply across the United States.
The government took over the mortgage companies.
Unemployment benefits were raised for homeowners.
section_a.explanation: 第1段：大量房主无力还贷，拥有这些贷款的公司及其子公司、股东因此损失了大笔资金，随之而来的裁员与解聘又冲击了美国就业市场。

section_a.question: Who were the “99ers”?
options: People who earned less than 99 dollars a week.
People who had exhausted the maximum 99 weeks of unemployment insurance benefits they could claim.
People who lost their jobs at the age of 99.
People who had worked for 99 months without a break.
section_a.explanation: 第4段：他们自称“99ers”，因为他们已经用完了可以领取的最长99周失业保险金。

section_a.question: What did the unemployment benefits mean to the jobless people?
options: They covered the cost of a university education.
They allowed them to start their own businesses.
They were a lifeline that let them keep a roof over their heads and pay their bills.
They helped them buy new cars and houses.
section_a.explanation: 第5段：失业救济金是“a lifeline”，让失业者至少维持正常生活的表象——有住处、给车加油、付电费和电话费。

section_a.question: Why does the author say Sue spent each day like a ping pong ball?
options: She kept moving from one city to another.
She played table tennis to forget her troubles.
She was passed between different employers.
She went back and forth between resolve and despair.
section_a.explanation: 第7段：每天像乒乓球一样在“resolve（决心）”与“despair（绝望）”之间来回摇摆。

section_b.question: What are “economic bubbles”?
options: A government policy that keeps prices stable over a long period.
A sudden fall in the price of oil and other commodities.
A period when banks refuse to lend money to homeowners.
A situation in which excessive investment drives prices far beyond an item’s intrinsic value.
section_b.explanation: 第1段定义：对商品、证券、房地产或收藏品的过度投资把价格推高到远超其内在价值的程度，其必然结果是暴涨后崩盘。

section_b.question: What is the “negative feedback mechanism” of the economy?
options: Rising prices encourage greater production or greater willingness of owners to sell, which pushes prices down.
Speculators become nervous and stop investing in the market.
The government raises interest rates to control prices.
Buyers refuse to pay more than the intrinsic value of an asset.
section_b.explanation: 第2段：价格上涨会促使产量增加，或使持有者更愿意出售，这两种情况都能把价格压低，即“负反馈”机制。

section_b.question: What is the “greater fool theory”?
options: Fools always lose money in the stock market.
Buyers justify their purchases by believing they will find someone who will pay even more.
Only foolish people invest in real estate.
Prices fall because buyers are foolish.
section_b.explanation: 第3段：买家以“总会有更大的傻瓜出更高价”来自我辩解，买盘彼此传染，把价格进一步推高。

section_b.question: How is “herd mentality” defined here?
options: Investors carefully study a company’s future profits.
Brokers refuse to buy when prices are rising.
Too many brokers rush to buy, driving prices to unrealistic levels.
Companies sell their assets to healthier companies.
section_b.explanation: 第6段：herd mentality 指众多经纪人蜂拥买入，像温度计里的水银一样把价格抬到不切实际的高度。

section_c.question: How do readers borrow books from the sharing bookstore in Hefei?
options: By paying a monthly fee at the bookstore counter
By scanning a QR code after paying a deposit
By leaving an ID card with the shop assistant
By ordering the books online and waiting for delivery
section_c.explanation: 第2段：合肥三孝口新华书店要求读者下载App、在线交押金，再扫码借书。

section_c.question: About how many books were borrowed and returned in the bookstore's first month?
options: Nearly 8,000
Nearly 18,000
Nearly 80,000
Nearly 800,000
section_c.explanation: 第2段：书店开业第一个月，借出和归还的图书接近8万册（nearly 80,000）。

section_c.question: Why does the book lover prefer the sharing bookstore to a library?
options: Its books are much cheaper to buy
Its reading rooms are quieter and larger
Its staff know more about literature
Its shelves are updated more frequently
section_c.explanation: 第4段：这位爱书者认为，与图书馆相比，大书店更新书架更频繁，读者更容易读到喜欢的书。

section_c.question: Why do some experts doubt the “book sharing” services?
options: Because they still charge deposits and fines
Because they are run by foreign companies
Because they offer too few books to readers
Because they will replace public libraries
section_c.explanation: 第7段：有专家认为部分“图书共享”只是噱头，只要还要交押金或罚款，就与以往小书店的借书服务无异，并非真正的共享。

section_a.title: Surviving an economic crisis
section_a.passage: The economic slump that so many people suffered through originated in the United States, with a regulatory failure of mortgages rated less risky than they turned out to be. As large numbers of homeowners proved unable to repay their loans, the companies that owned the loans (as well as their subsidiaries and shareholders) lost sizable amounts of money. The effects of these drastic losses soon spiraled into the U.S. job market as lay-offs and terminations. The rebound was slow in coming. Many people experienced long months of financial difficulties just like the character in this story. Facing tenant eviction after several months of unpaid rent, Sue Johnson packed up whatever she could fit into her two-door automobile and drove out of town. She wound up at a motel, putting down the $260 she had managed to scrape together from friends and from selling her living room set. It was all the money Sue had after her unemployment benefits had expired. She faced life as a migrant, a previously unimaginable situation for a woman who, not that long before, had held a corporate job in a metropolitan city and had been enrolled in a graduate business school. Sue knew that, in all likelihood, she would end up living in her car. She was part of a hard-luck group of jobless people who called themselves “99ers”, because they had exhausted the maximum 99 weeks of unemployment insurance benefits that they could claim. Long-term unemployment was at record levels. Modest payments of unemployment benefits were a lifeline that enabled people who were out of work to maintain at least an appearance of normalcy, keeping a roof over their heads, putting gas in their cars, and paying electric and phone bills. Without the checks, people like Sue, who had once been a director of client services at a technology company, began to tumble over the economic cliff. The last remnants of their former working-class or middle-class lives were gone, and all of them faced unsure futures. When Sue received her last unemployment check, she felt a wave of profound grief. With no income to deposit, Sue’s checking account went into a negative balance. Her car was on the verge of being repossessed. And, the constant harassment of the financing company for her car loan added to her daily stress. Each day, like a ping pong ball, Sue went back and forth between resolve and despair. It was a sickening plunge considering that only a short year and a half before, Sue had earned $56,000 a year at her old job, enjoyed vacationing in places like Mexico and the Caribbean, and started business school at an excellent university. Initially, Sue had tried to finish her university certification remotely, but finally dropped out because of the stress from her sinking finances. She applied for every possible job in the employment spectrum, from minimum-wage retail jobs to director positions. Sue should have been evicted from her two-bedroom apartment for non-payment several months before she was, but, thankfully, the process was delayed by paperwork and bureaucracy. Eventually, the bureaucracy caught up with her, and she was given 10 days to leave her apartment for good. She had no choice but to comply. That last day of her old life, Sue wept as she drove away. She wondered if she would ever again be able to reclaim that life of comfort and respect. She fell into complete despair and didn’t know what would happen to her next. Friends came to her aid. One friend wired her $200 while she was driving away from her old apartment, enabling her to find refuge in a motel along the way. But Sue worried there wouldn’t be any more charity that she desperately needed. Helped by gas cards donated by a church, Sue decided to return to her hometown. She figured the health-care safety net there was better, as well as the job market. She contacted a local shelter but learned there was a waiting list. Welfare was not an option, because she didn’t have young children. And, Sue knew that none of her three adult sons were in a position to help her. “I knew the only help I was going to get was from me myself,” Sue said. “I thought to myself: I have to take care of myself. I really, really need to get work. I need a job. I don’t want to be seen as a parasite.” Sue’s motel room was depressing. Lining the shelves underneath the television were her food supplies: rice and noodles that she mixed with water in the motel’s ice bucket and heated up in a microwave, peanut butter and jelly, a loaf of white bread – the subsistence of a desperate person. Sue’s days were spent surfing Internet job indexes and applying for jobs where the silent “No”, “No”, “No” led to a feeling of helplessness. Sue had all new problems and obstacles to deal with, too, like what to do for an address for job applications. She worried about what would happen when her cell phone was cut off for non-payment, and calls to her number would disappear into an invisible world she could not reach. Finally, an old friend sent Sue a ray of hope, a small miracle: $300 cash – just enough for another brutal week of financial struggles.

section_b.title: Economic bubbles: causes and conditions
section_b.passage: Economic bubbles occur when, for any number of reasons, excessive investment in commodities (such as oil), securities (such as stocks and bonds), real estate, or collectibles drives up prices well beyond the item’s intrinsic value. The inevitable result of this boom in price is a crash or bust. The price falls sharply once it becomes clear that it has grown far beyond the purchasing power of potential customers. Speculators risk money in such investments because they hope that the price of an asset they purchase will quickly increase. Since most speculators are nervous about where they invest their money, bubbles are by no means the norm. After all, every investment entails the risk that it is overpriced. Speculators also know that rising prices will encourage either greater production of a commodity or greater willingness of current owners to sell. Either of these conditions can serve as a “negative feedback” mechanism that adjusts prices downward. As an analogy, think of negative feedback like your eyes. As the light gets brighter, your pupils get smaller and let in less light. But what if, instead, your eyes worked as a “positive feedback” mechanism? In sunlight, your pupils would open wide and damage your eyes. Economic bubbles occur when prices trending sharply upward spur positive, rather than negative, feedback. For whatever reason (fear of shortages, greed, an excessively optimistic attitude toward the future, or flaws in the analysis of an asset’s underlying value), buyers believe that the value of the asset will continue to rise. If the price rises, overly enthusiastic speculators buy more, or those who missed out on the lower price flock to buy before the price rises any higher. The foremost explanation is the “greater fool theory”: Buyers justify their purchases by assuring themselves they will find “a greater fool” who will pay even more. Buyer enthusiasm infects other buyers, amplifying the effect even further. Under the right conditions, prices can reach dizzying heights before falling. One famous example is the tulip-buying bubble which happened in the Netherlands in the 1630s when a single tulip bulb could cost a year’s salary. Most bubbles are easily assimilated or averted by an elastic market. Provided the bubble is small enough, the losers earn wisdom in retrospect, and the winners earn a lot of money. But the effects of a bubble might become cumulative if many owners of an overpriced asset feel rich and spend foolishly, especially in a period of deregulation. Imagine this: You buy a house for $200,000, for which you borrowed $160,000 beforehand. You have $40,000 in equity in the house. Over the next five years, the market appraisal rises to $500,000. Now you have $340,000 in equity ($500,000 – $160,000), so you borrow another $240,000 from a bank using this equity to secure the loan. You still have $100,000 in equity in your home, and you have $240,000 to spend. You suddenly feel less need to be economical with your purchases and allocate more money for things like a vacation home and a new car. But equity is not revenue. The market holds long enough for you to spend the money. Then it crashes and the value of your home falls to $325,000. Now you have negative equity and owe the bank $400,000. So you default on your loan and give your house, car, and vacation home to the bank. If this situation is widespread, it can culminate in the failure of those banks and a severe blow to the lending needed to grow the economy. There are also stock market bubbles. In a normal market, investors buy stock in a company because they anticipate that future profits will become dividends and they believe the value of the company’s assets will increase. Sometimes, though, a “herd mentality” sets in and too many brokers rush to buy, driving prices like mercury up a thermometer to levels that prove unrealistic. Eventually, it becomes clear that further increases are not forthcoming and price deterioration develops, followed by a swift drop. When this happens to too many companies in aggregate, it is called a stock market crash. A striking example of a stock market bubble is the “dot-com” bubble. The buzz about the economic possibilities of the Internet encouraged investors to fund the creation of many dot-com companies – too many, it turned out. For several years, dozens of entrepreneurs sought to duplicate for themselves the results of those that had come before. Many investors envisaged wealth for any business with a website that could advertise on TV or billboards, even if its actual services were ambiguous. Instead, on March 10, 2000, the dot-com boom reached its peak when the stock index hit 5,132.52. Over the next two and a half years, the index dropped to as low as 1,108.49. Very few companies bucked the trend. Most had blundered into awful financial difficulties, selling off their assets to healthier companies. Bubbles are not limited to the arena of real estate or “get-rich” stock offerings. In the 1990s, a series of stuffed animal toys became such a fad that speculators bought up large quantities, assuming that their value as collectibles would continue to rise. Did anyone make money on that fad? If you check out their prices on an online auction site, you can decide whether any of these sellers have struck it rich.

section_c.title: The sharing economy turns a new page with books
section_c.passage: From sharing bicycles to sharing cars, China’s sharing economy has now swept into the book industry. Book-sharing services have been launched in cities such as Shanghai, Suzhou, and Hefei. Sanxiaokou Xinhua Bookstore in Hefei of Anhui Province, which declared itself the “first sharing bookstore in the world”, opened to the public in July 2017. Readers need to download an app and pay a deposit online. Then they can borrow books by scanning the QR code. During the first month of the bookstore’s operation, the number of books borrowed and returned reached nearly 80,000. In addition, banks are also involved in the sharing economy, offering book-lending services. Users can borrow books after registering through the official account on social media and paying the deposit. “It doesn’t matter if books are sold or shared; as long as they are read, they benefit society. Culture can be delivered in different forms,” said a woman who is a book lover and likes the sharing of books. “Compared with borrowing books from libraries, the large bookstores update their shelves more frequently, so readers can enjoy their favorite books more easily.” A national reading survey showed that on average, Chinese people read less than eight books a year. Jumping on the bandwagon of the sharing economy may tempt young people to return to bookstores first, and help develop their reading habits. However, there is still no specific definition of “book sharing”, and many problems need to be resolved in the actual operation. Some experts claim that some “book sharing” is just a gimmick, the same stuff with a new label. From a business perspective, they think that today’s “book sharing” is no different from the book-lending services some small bookstores have long offered. This is not real sharing as long as the book-sharing services require a deposit or impose a fine. Some people claim that the “sharing bookstore” is only a concept, just like the previous “flowing bookstall” on the street, which can also be labeled as “sharing”. Many people believe that “book sharing” is a new business attempt in the book industry and the public should give it a chance. There is a long way to go, for “book sharing”.

questions.question: Why did Sue decide to return to her hometown?
options: She believed the health-care safety net and the job market were better there.
She had inherited a house there.
Her three adult sons invited her to live with them.
A local shelter had promised her a place to stay.
questions.explanation: 第13段：她认为家乡的医疗保障网和就业市场都更好；她联系当地收容所，却得知还要排队等位。

questions.question: Why did Sue think the only help she was going to get was from herself?
options: She did not know that any welfare program existed.
She had no young children, so welfare was not an option, and none of her three adult sons could help her.
Her friends and sons had all refused to help her.
She was too proud to accept help from a church.
questions.explanation: 第13、14段：她没有年幼子女，不符合福利救济条件；三个成年儿子也无力帮她，所以她说“only help ... from me myself”。

questions.question: What new problems and obstacles did Sue have to face when she applied for a job?
options: She was too old to be considered by employers.
She had no clothes suitable for a job interview.
She had no address for job applications and her cell phone might be cut off.
She could not read or write well enough to fill in forms.
questions.explanation: 第16段：她求职时没有地址可用；手机因欠费被停机后，打到她号码的电话会“消失”在她无法触及的世界里。

questions.question: What does the author intend to tell us by Sue’s story?
options: Charities are more helpful than government programs.
Unemployment benefits should be abolished.
Moving back to one’s hometown is the best solution.
An economic crisis can push an ordinary person with a decent job into deep poverty and despair.
questions.explanation: 全文以 Sue 从公司主管沦落到住汽车旅馆的经历，说明经济危机如何一步步侵蚀普通人的收入、居住、教育与信心。

questions.question: When you ______ clothes, you not only free up room in your closet but also help people in need.
options: donate
comply
reclaim
expire
questions.explanation: 句意为“捐出衣物”：donate 捐赠；comply 须与 with 搭配表示“遵守”，expire 指“到期”，reclaim 指“取回”，均不合语境。

questions.question: The young man watched his financial life ______ downward just when he thought he had overcome the obstacles which had dominated his past.
options: reclaim
spiral
donate
expire
questions.explanation: spiral downward 表示“（财务状况）不断恶化、急剧下滑”，watch sb./sth. do 后接动词原形。

questions.question: Setbacks are the things in life that test your ______ to achieve your goals.
options: subsistence
eviction
resolve
harassment
questions.explanation: test your resolve 意为“考验你的决心”；resolve 作名词表示“决心、决意”。

questions.question: The company was reportedly going bankrupt and this would result in ______ of thousands of employees.
options: deposits
evictions
obstacles
lay-offs
questions.explanation: lay-off 意为“解雇、裁员”，此处用复数 lay-offs：result in lay-offs of thousands of employees（导致数千名员工被裁）。

questions.question: She has always lived a life of wealth and doesn’t understand that many things she is used to are unimaginable luxuries to people on ______ wages.
options: subsistence
harassment
resolve
termination
questions.explanation: subsistence wages 指“勉强糊口的工资”，与前面的 wealth、luxuries 形成鲜明对比。

questions.question: The social media giant has announced that it is to roll out new tools to protect its users from ______ or unwanted contact from other people.
options: eviction
harassment
deposit
expiration
questions.explanation: harassment 意为“骚扰、侵扰”，与后面的 unwanted contact 并列，说明要保护用户免受骚扰。

In the 1990s, a series of stuffed animal toys became such a fad that speculators bought up large quantities, assuming that their value as collectibles would continue to rise. Did anyone make money on that fad? If you check out their prices on an online auction site, you can decide whether any of these sellers have struck it rich.

questions.question: What is a “stock market crash”?
options: A single company’s shares lose value quickly.
Investors receive fewer dividends than expected.
The government closes the stock market for a period.
Price deterioration and a swift drop happen to too many companies in aggregate.
questions.explanation: 第6段末：当大量公司同时出现价格恶化和暴跌时，就称为股市崩盘（stock market crash）。

questions.question: What is the “dot-com bubble”?
options: A stock market bubble in which too many Internet companies were funded and the index later collapsed.
A bubble in the price of tulip bulbs in the Netherlands.
A bubble caused by the shortage of computer equipment.
A period when no investors were willing to fund new businesses.
questions.explanation: 第7段：互联网前景的炒作让投资者资助了过多网络公司，股指在2000年3月10日见顶5,132.52后，两年半内跌至1,108.49。

questions.question: Which of the following is the consequence of economic bubbles?
options: Panic buying.
A crash in price.
Excessive investment.
Raised purchasing power.
questions.explanation: 第1段：价格暴涨（boom in price）的必然结果是“a crash or bust”，即价格暴跌。

questions.question: Why are economic bubbles by no means the norm?
options: Speculators are nervous about their investment.
People usually know the intrinsic value of an asset.
Manufacturers are reluctant to expand production for fear of risk.
Overpriced products are beyond the purchasing power of customers.
questions.explanation: 第2段：多数投机者对自己投资的对象心存不安，因此泡沫并非常态（by no means the norm）。

questions.question: In a positive feedback system, what would happen when prices increase sharply?
options: Speculators know the prices will fall in the near future.
Speculators are eager to sell their assets to make a profit.
Speculators become greedier and buy more assets.
Speculators become more united to get the best prices.
questions.explanation: 第3段：价格一涨，过度热情的投机者会买得更多，错过低价的人也会蜂拥而入，形成“正反馈”。

questions.question: The “greater fool theory” explains ______.
options: how prices reach dizzying heights
how people’s foolishness can be avoided
why buyers buy more than necessary
why speculators do not flock to the market
questions.explanation: 第3段：买家相信会有“更大的傻瓜”出更高价，这种心态互相传染，价格因而被推到令人眩晕的高位。

questions.question: What will happen when big economic bubbles occur?
options: The involved banks may fail.
You will be economical with your purchases.
The market can easily assimilate the bubbles.
The market can help the winners earn wisdom.
questions.explanation: 第5段：若负资产情况普遍，就可能“culminate in the failure of those banks”，并重创经济增长所需的信贷。

questions.question: The “herd mentality” explains ______.
options: how the stock market goes bust
what happens to a company in economic crises
how brokers drive the stock prices to unrealistic heights
how investors buy stock in a company in a reasonable way
questions.explanation: 第6段：herd mentality 指过多经纪人蜂拥买入，把股价推高到不切实际的水平。

questions.question: What do we know about the “dot-com” bubble?
options: The stock index dropped by about 40 percent in 2002.
Many companies ended up selling off their assets to other companies.
The investors were provided with false information about the business.
The stock index dropped to 1,108.49 right after the boom reached its peak.
questions.explanation: 第7段末：多数公司陷入严重财务困境，把资产出售给更健康的公司；股指是在两年半里逐步跌至1,108.49，并非见顶后立即暴跌。

questions.question: What can we learn from the text?
options: Economic bubbles reflect the laws of economics.
Economic bubbles often occur in the stock market.
Economic bubbles mostly result in very bad consequences.
Economic bubbles first appeared at the turn of the 21st century.
questions.explanation: 全文说明泡沫是过度投资、投机心理与市场反馈等经济规律共同作用的结果：泡沫不限于股市，多数可被弹性市场吸收，郁金香泡沫早在17世纪就已出现。

sentences.zh: 当前，中国实行更加积极主动的开放战略，构建面向全球的高标准自由贸易区网络，加快推进自由贸易试验区、海南自由贸易港建设。中国已成为140多个国家和地区的主要贸易伙伴，吸引外资和对外投资（outbound investment）居世界前列。未来，中国将不断推进高水平对外开放，提升贸易投资合作质量和水平，加快建设贸易强国。
sentences.en_reference: At present, China is pursuing a more proactive opening-up strategy, building a global network of high-standard free trade areas, and stepping up the development of pilot free trade zones and the Hainan Free Trade Port. China has become a major trading partner of more than 140 countries and regions, and ranks among the world’s leaders in both attracting foreign investment and making outbound investment. In the future, China will continue to advance high-standard opening-up, improve the quality and level of trade and investment cooperation, and move faster to build itself into a strong trading nation.

writing.prompt: Write an essay of no less than 140 words on the negative effects of staying up late. Develop your essay as a cause-and-effect essay: state your thesis in the introduction, present the effects in the body from the least to the most important, and restate your position in the conclusion.
outline: Introduction: Thesis statement – staying up late can do severe harm to us mainly in three aspects.
Body: Effect 1 – negative impacts on our physical health; Effect 2 – lower work efficiency; Effect 3 – mental stress.
Support each effect with details or examples from students’ daily life, and arrange them from the least to the most serious.
Conclusion: Staying up late is by no means a good choice for us.
